etymology: Hebrew Yanochah, “rest” or “resting-place”; a town on the eastern border of Ephraim, named in the tracing of the tribal line.
biblical_def: Janohah, “a resting-place,” was a town on the eastern border of Ephraim, named as the boundary bent along its course: “And the border went out toward the sea to Michmethah on the north side; and the border went about eastward unto Taanathshiloh, and passed by it on the east to Janohah” (Josh 16:6). It was one of the many landmarks by which the inheritance of Joseph was measured out, for “the lot of the children of Joseph fell from Jordan by Jericho” (Josh 16:1) and ran through hill and valley to the sea. The name, “rest,” is a sweet one for a border-town, and it turns the mind to the great theme of rest that runs through all the settling of the land. Israel entered Canaan that the LORD might give her rest from all her enemies round about; Joshua’s very name is a form of the name of Him who gives the true rest. Yet the rest of Canaan was only a shadow; there remaineth a rest, a sabbath-keeping, for the people of God, which Joshua’s conquest could not fully give. Janohah, a little resting-place on Ephraim’s border, points beyond itself to that abiding rest into which the weary and heavy-laden enter by coming to Christ, who says, Come unto me, and I will give you rest.

etymology: Hebrew Ataroth, “crowns”; a town on the border of Ephraim; distinct from Ataroth in Gad beyond Jordan.
biblical_def: Ataroth, “crowns,” was a town on the border of Ephraim, named as the line came down from Janohah: “And it went down from Janohah to Ataroth, and to Naarath, and came to Jericho, and went out at Jordan” (Josh 16:7). It is to be distinguished from Ataroth in the land of Gad beyond Jordan, built by the Reubenites and Gadites; several towns bore this common name meaning crowns. The name is a rich one for a town of the house of Joseph, that most blessed of the tribes, of whom Jacob said the blessings were on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren. Ephraim and Manasseh were the ten thousands and thousands that pushed the peoples to the ends of the earth (Deu 33:17). Ataroth, a crown-town of that blessed house, preaches the crowning goodness of God to His people. He crowneth the year with His goodness, He crowneth His saints with lovingkindness and tender mercies, and He has laid up a crown of righteousness, a crown of life, an incorruptible crown, for them that love Him and are faithful unto death. The little town of crowns is a token that the God who blessed Joseph delights to crown His people with His grace and to bring them at last to glory.

etymology: Hebrew Mikmethath, of uncertain meaning; a landmark on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, lying before Shechem.
biblical_def: Michmethah was a boundary landmark between Ephraim and Manasseh, lying over against Shechem: the border “went out toward the sea to Michmethah on the north side” (Josh 16:6), and again, “the coast of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethah, that lieth before Shechem” (Josh 17:7). It stood near the great central sanctuary-city of Shechem, where Abraham first built an altar in the land, where Jacob bought a field and dug a well, where Joshua gathered all Israel to renew the covenant between mounts Ebal and Gerizim, and where the bones of Joseph were buried. To lie before Shechem was to lie in the heart of the promises. Michmethah, an obscure boundary-mark, preaches the honour of the borderland near holy ground. The line between the two tribes of Joseph ran past the place of covenant-renewal, as if to remind them that all their inheritance was held under the covenant sworn at Shechem: to serve the LORD and put away strange gods. The believer, too, lives all his life before the place of covenant; every boundary of his days is drawn near the altar and the promises, that he may remember whose he is and whom he serves.

etymology: Hebrew Tappuach, “apple” or “apple-tree”; a town on the border of Manasseh and Ephraim; the town belonged to Ephraim though the land about it was Manasseh’s.
biblical_def: This Tappuah, “apple-town,” lay on the border between Manasseh and Ephraim, and its case is instructive: “Now Manasseh had the land of Tappuah: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim” (Josh 17:8); the border “went out from Tappuah westward unto the river Kanah” (Josh 16:8). Thus the fields round about were reckoned to Manasseh, but the town itself to Ephraim — a nice division that shows how carefully the inheritance was allotted, tribe distinguished from tribe even where their lands ran together. This town is distinct from Tappuah in the low country of Judah and from En-tappuah. The name, from the apple, speaks of fruitfulness and sweet savour; the apple-tree among the trees of the wood is the figure the bride uses of her beloved in the Song, in whose shadow she sat with great delight, and whose fruit was sweet to her taste. Tappuah, an apple-town on the border of blessed Joseph, preaches the fruitfulness God gives and the sweetness of communion with Christ, the true apple-tree, under whose shadow the soul finds shelter and whose fruit is the joy of the redeemed.

etymology: Hebrew Taanath Shiloh, perhaps “the approach to Shiloh”; a town on the eastern border of Ephraim, near the road to Shiloh.
biblical_def: Taanath-shiloh was a town on the eastern border of Ephraim, named as the tribal line ran its course: the border “went about eastward unto Taanathshiloh, and passed by it on the east to Janohah” (Josh 16:6). Its name binds it to Shiloh, the place where the tabernacle of the congregation was set up when the land was subdued, and where the ark of God rested through the days of the judges until the sad day it was carried into battle and taken by the Philistines. If the name means “the approach to Shiloh,” then this town stood on the way that pilgrims trod to the house of God. Taanath-shiloh preaches the blessedness of the road that leads to worship. Once Shiloh was the centre of Israel’s life, where the tribes came up to keep the feasts and Hannah prayed and Samuel ministered; and the approach to it was hallowed by the feet of the faithful going up to appear before the LORD. Yet Shiloh was forsaken for Israel’s sin, and God made it a warning, bidding the people go and see what He did to Shiloh. The approach-town remains a call to tread the way to God’s house with reverence, and a warning that privilege despised is privilege withdrawn.

etymology: Hebrew Chepher, “a pit” or “a well”; a royal Canaanite city west of Jordan whose king Joshua smote; the land of Hepher lay in Solomon’s administrative district; distinct from Gath-hepher.
biblical_def: Hepher was a royal Canaanite city west of Jordan, one of the thirty-one kings Joshua overthrew in the conquest: “The king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one” (Josh 12:17). In Solomon’s day the surrounding country was still known as the land of Hepher, reckoned to one of his officers’ districts: to Ben-hesed “pertained Sochoh, and all the land of Hepher” (1Ki 4:10). This place is distinct from Gath-hepher, the town of the prophet Jonah in Zebulun. The name means a pit or a digging, perhaps a well. Hepher takes its place in the long roll of kings whom the LORD gave into Israel’s hand, for it was not by their own sword that Israel got the land in possession, nor did their own arm save them, but the right hand of God and the light of His countenance, because He had a favour unto them. The fall of the king of Hepher preaches the completeness of God’s victory over the powers that held the promised land. Every petty king was cast down that the seed of Abraham might inherit; and so the true Joshua overthrows all the powers that hold His people’s inheritance, that they might enter into the rest prepared and reign with Him.

etymology: Hebrew Tebets, perhaps “brightness”; a fortified town near Shechem where Abimelech the usurper was slain by a woman’s millstone.
biblical_def: Thebez was a fortified town near Shechem, remembered as the place where Abimelech, the bramble-king who slew his seventy brethren to make himself ruler, met his end: “Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and encamped against Thebez, and took it” (Judg 9:50). But when he drew near to burn the strong tower into which the people had fled, “a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head, and all to brake his skull” (Judg 9:53); and he begged his armour-bearer to run him through, that men might not say a woman slew him. So the LORD rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, and the curse of Jotham came upon him. Thebez preaches the certain judgment of God upon usurped and bloody power. Abimelech grasped the kingdom by murder, ruled by cruelty, and fell by a woman’s hand and a broken millstone, brought down in a moment from his height. God is not mocked; whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. The proud who exalt themselves by blood and violence are cast down, often by the weakest instrument, that all may know the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men and putteth down the mighty from their seats.

etymology: Hebrew Tabbath, of uncertain meaning; a place east of Jordan to which the Midianite host fled before Gideon’s three hundred.
biblical_def: Tabbath marked the far reach of the Midianite flight when the LORD routed their vast host by Gideon’s three hundred: “And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Bethshittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath” (Judg 7:22). Gideon’s men had no weapons in their hands but trumpets and lamps hidden in pitchers; at the breaking of the pitchers and the blast of the trumpets and the cry, The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon, the Midianites turned their swords upon one another and fled in the night as far as Tabbath. The place preaches the same lesson as the whole story of Gideon: that the LORD saves without the might of men, lest Israel vaunt herself and say, Mine own hand hath saved me. God had thinned the army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred on purpose, that the victory might be plainly His. Tabbath, the limit of the enemy’s panic flight, is a monument to salvation by the sword of the LORD, won not by numbers or arms but by the God who sends confusion among His enemies and gives His people the victory while they hold their ground and trust His word.

The principle to recover is that the LORD saves without the might of men. He thinned Gideon’s army from thousands to three hundred on purpose, lest Israel say, Mine own hand hath saved me. At the breaking of the pitchers and the cry, The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon, the host fled to Tabbath. The place is a monument that victory is God’s, given to those who hold their ground and trust His word.

etymology: Hebrew Tsarethan (also Zartanah, Zererath); a place in the Jordan valley near which the waters of Jordan stood up in a heap at Israel’s crossing.
biblical_def: Zaretan was a place in the Jordan valley, named at one of the greatest moments in Israel’s history, when the LORD divided the waters of Jordan before the ark that His people might pass over into the land: “That the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam, that is beside Zaretan” (Josh 3:16). As the feet of the priests bearing the ark touched the brim of the water, the river was cut off, heaped up as far as Zaretan, and all Israel passed over on dry ground. This was the LORD’s doing, a second Red Sea, that all the people of the earth might know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and that Israel might fear Him for ever. Zaretan, where the waters piled up, preaches the power of God to open a way where there is no way. As He drove back the sea for the fathers and the river for the children, so He removes every barrier before His people when the hour of His purpose is come. The ark went before, and the flood gave place; and the believer, following the Lord who went down into the deep waters of death and rose again, passes through every Jordan into the promised inheritance, kept dry-shod by the power of God.

etymology: Hebrew Har Tsemarayim, “mount of the two fleeces” or “double woollen height”; a mountain in the hill country of Ephraim from which Abijah of Judah proclaimed God’s covenant to Jeroboam’s host; distinct from the town Zemaraim.
biblical_def: Mount Zemaraim was a height in the hill country of Ephraim from which Abijah king of Judah addressed the army of Jeroboam before battle: “And Abijah stood up upon mount Zemaraim, which is in mount Ephraim, and said, Hear me, thou Jeroboam, and all Israel” (2Ch 13:4). This is a mountain, distinct from the town Zemaraim in Benjamin of the same name. From that height Abijah declared the great matter at issue: that the LORD God of Israel had given the kingdom to David and his sons by a covenant of salt for ever, that Judah kept the appointed priesthood and the ordained worship, while Jeroboam had cast out the priests of the LORD and made molten calves. Though Jeroboam ambushed Judah before and behind, “the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers.” Mount Zemaraim preaches the power of a right confession joined to true reliance. Abijah’s sermon from the mount was no empty boast; it rested on the covenant of God and the true worship, and God honoured it with victory. The believer learns that the ground of confidence in every spiritual battle is not his own strength but the covenant of God and faithfulness to His appointed truth and worship; they that so rely upon the LORD shall prevail.
